title: Chris Hansen Slams Robert Pattinson’s ‘Primetime’: “Not a Fan” – Shocking TV Critique】
body:
The former “To Catch a Predator” anchor Chris Hansen has publicly dismissed Robert Pattinson’s portrayal of him in A24’s newly released dramatization “Primetime,” calling the film a “fever dream” and assigning the lead performance a failing “D” grade. In an unfiltered interview on his own podcast, Hansen unpacked his frustration with what he described as an unauthorized, sensationalized retelling of a narrow slice of his personal and professional life, and he warned audiences that the movie bears little resemblance to the reality he experienced.

“Primetime” arrived on the streaming circuit after months of speculation and a very public back‑and‑forth between Hansen and A24, the independent studio that produced the film. The studio has a reputation for championing bold, auteur‑driven projects, but it has also courted controversy by tackling real‑world subjects without securing the explicit consent of those depicted. In this case, the studio’s decision to dramatize the 2010–2012 period when Hansen’s “To Catch a Predator” team conducted high‑profile sting operations sparked immediate criticism from the former journalist, who argued that the film exploits his legacy for shock value rather than insight.

During the podcast, Hansen detailed how the script was assembled from public footage, news reports, and second‑hand accounts, noting that none of the key participants—himself, the producers, or the victims featured in the original series—were consulted. He said the resulting narrative feels more like a stylized thriller than a factual recounting, with the filmmakers employing hyper‑real lighting, disorienting sound design, and a non‑linear structure that, in his view, “turns a serious investigative effort into a nightmarish carnival ride.” The “fever dream” comment reflects his belief that the film’s aesthetic choices obscure the gravity of the original sting operations, which led to numerous arrests and sparked national debate over entrapment and media ethics.

Critics who have seen the film echo some of Hansen’s concerns, pointing out that Pattinson’s performance, while technically polished, leans heavily into a caricature of the veteran journalist. Reviewers note that the actor adopts a detached, almost sardonic tone, which may be intended to highlight the absurdity of the situation but ultimately distances viewers from the emotional stakes. By assigning a “D” grade, Hansen underscored his disappointment not only with the casting but also with the broader creative direction, suggesting that the film sacrifices nuance for sensationalism.

The controversy also raises questions about the evolving relationship between documentary subjects and the entertainment industry. As streaming platforms continue to mine real‑life events for dramatic content, the line between factual representation and artistic license becomes increasingly blurred. Hansen’s outspoken criticism could prompt studios to reconsider consent protocols, especially when dealing with living individuals whose reputations are at stake. Legal experts note that while public figures have limited recourse against dramatizations, a pattern of disregard for subjects’ input may invite lawsuits or, at the very least, public backlash that can affect a studio’s brand.

Looking ahead, “Primetime” may serve as a flashpoint for a broader conversation about responsible storytelling in an era of rapid content production. If audiences respond negatively to the film’s approach, studios might be compelled to adopt more collaborative models, involving the people whose stories they adapt from the outset. For Hansen, the episode appears to have reinforced his resolve to protect his legacy and to challenge media portrayals that he feels misrepresent the truth. Whether that advocacy will translate into formal action or further public commentary remains to be seen, but the debate sparked by “Primetime” is unlikely to fade quickly.
